brave-llmcontext.snippet:
# How Long Do Eye Drops Last? Expiry and Storage
## Key takeaways
- There is no single discard date for eye drops. Real US labels disagree with each other: TheraTears says 45 days after opening, Refresh Tears, Oasis Tears PF and Systane Ultra PF say 90, and some labels give no period at all.
- The "do not reuse, once opened discard" line on single-use vials is not a manufacturer preference. It is wording the FDA requires on single-use ophthalmic containers.
## Discard after opening: the numbers do not agree
| Product | What the label says |
| --- | --- |
| TheraTears Lubricant Eye Drops | Discard 45 days after opening |
| Refresh Tears | Discard 90 days after opening |
| Refresh Tears PF | Discard 90 days after opening |
| Oasis Tears PF | Discard 90 days after opening |
| Systane Ultra PF | Discard 90 days after opening |
| Blink Tears | No discard period stated on the label |
## Single-use vials, and the question everyone actually has
Preservative-free vials carry a required warning. Federal regulation sets the wording for single-use ophthalmic containers: "To avoid contamination, do not touch tip of container to any surface. Do not reuse. Once opened, discard."
Compare that with the wording the same regulation requires on multi-use containers: "To avoid contamination, do not touch tip of container to any surface. Replace cap after using." The reuse sentence is deliberately absent. That difference is the whole point of a vial.

jina.snippet:
## Key takeaways

*   There is no single discard date for eye drops. Real US labels disagree with each other: TheraTears says 45 days after opening, Refresh Tears, Oasis Tears PF and Systane Ultra PF say 90, and some labels give no period at all.
*   The "do not reuse, once opened discard" line on single-use vials is not a manufacturer preference. It is wording the FDA requires on single-use ophthalmic containers.
*   Preservative-free multi-dose bottles do not buy you longer in use. The ones we checked state the same 90 days as a preserved bottle.
*   The dropper tip is the part that picks up contamination, more than the liquid inside, and the organisms found on it are ordinary skin and eyelid bacteria.
*   Labels specify room temperature, commonly 59 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit. None of the labels we checked tells you to refrigerate.

## The short version

Read your own bottle. That sounds like a dodge, and it is not: we checked the FDA labels for seven artificial tears sold in the United States and they do not agree with one another. Any article that gives you one number for all eye drops is telling you about one product and hoping it generalises.

What follows is what the labels and the regulations actually say, and where they say nothing at all.

## The expiry date on an unopened bottle

An unopened bottle carries an expiration date, and the labels tell you to respect it. Refresh Tears puts it plainly in its Other information section: "Use before expiration date marked on container." Optase Dry Eye Intense single-dose units carry "Do not use after the expiry date shown on the pack."

One practical wrinkle catches people out. Federal labeling rules allow the date for single-dose containers packed in cartons to appear on the carton rather than on the container itself. So if you tear a strip of vials off and throw the box away, you may have thrown away the only expiry date you had. Keep the carton, or write the date on the strip.

Yes, and there are two different dates at work: the expiration date printed on an unopened bottle, and a discard period that starts the day you open it. The second one is set by the manufacturer for that specific product, and US labels range from 45 days to 90 days to no period at all.

The growth of preservative-free ophthalmic therapies has transformed the treatment landscape for patients managing conditions such as dry eye disease and glaucoma, as well as those recovering from ophthalmic procedures who may be sensitive to preservatives.  
As demand for preservative-free eye drops grows, so does the use of single-use delivery formats designed to protect product quality, minimize contamination risk and support patient safety.

## Key takeaways

- There is no single discard date for eye drops. Real US labels disagree with each other: TheraTears says 45 days after opening, Refresh Tears, Oasis Tears PF and Systane Ultra PF say 90, and some labels give no period at all.
- The "do not reuse, once opened discard" line on single-use vials is not a manufacturer preference. It is wording the FDA requires on single-use ophthalmic containers.
- Preservative-free multi-dose bottles do not buy you longer in use. The ones we checked state the same 90 days as a preserved bottle.
- The dropper tip is the part that picks up contamination, more than the liquid inside, and the organisms found on it are ordinary skin and eyelid bacteria.
- Labels specify room temperature, commonly 59 to 77 degrees Fahrenheit. None of the labels we checked tells you to refrigerate.

seltz.snippet:
## What Does The 30-Day Rule Mean For Eye Drops?

September 9, 2026

HEALTH · 18 MIN READ

Written by **Cured Pharmacy**

Published on 9 September 2026

★★★★★

Medically reviewed by

Tarun Kumar, Prescribing Pharmacist (GPhC 2233073)

Last reviewed: 17 November 2026

If you have ever picked up a bottle of eye drops and noticed a small "28 days after opening" or "30 days after opening" label on the side, you may have wondered whether it actually matters or whether it is just the manufacturer being overly cautious. Many people in the UK use the same bottle for weeks, or even months, beyond that date without giving it a second thought. But there is genuine clinical reasoning behind this guidance, and ignoring it can carry real risks for your eye health. Whether you are using antibiotic drops for an infection, lubricating drops for dry eyes, or anti-allergy drops during hay fever season, understanding this rule properly could save you a great deal of discomfort, and possibly prevent a more serious problem from developing.

Last updated: 17 November 2026 · Prices checked: 17 November 2026 · Next review: 17 May 2027

## Summary

The 30-day rule for eye drops is a safety guideline that limits how long a bottle of eye drops should be used after it has been opened. Once opened, the preservatives in most eye drops begin to lose their antimicrobial effectiveness, and the bottle itself can become a source of bacterial or fungal contamination, even if it looks and smells perfectly fine.

- Most multi-dose eye drops carry a 28 or 30-day discard period after first opening.
- This rule exists because preservatives degrade over time, leaving drops vulnerable to microbial growth.
- Preservative-free eye drops in single-use vials should be discarded immediately after each use.
- Using contaminated drops can cause or worsen eye infections, including serious ones.
- Antibiotic eye drops like chloramphenicol have specific usage periods

tavily.title: Single-Use Ophthalmic Vials: Why Recapping Doesn’t Restore Sterility
tavily.snippet:
Summary: Patients should administer the medication as directed and discard the vial after use, even if liquid remains.

Full answer: Single-use ophthalmic products are intended to be opened when needed, used according to the product directions, and then discarded. An opened vial should not be saved for later simply because medication remains inside. Patients should always follow the product labeling and instructions provided by their pharmacist, physician, or other healthcare professional. [...] Full answer: A single-use ophthalmic vial contains medication intended for one administration rather than repeated use over time. The unopened container provides a sterile barrier that helps protect the medication from contamination. Once the vial is opened, that barrier is compromised, so any remaining medication should be discarded according to the product instructions.

Why are single-use vials commonly used for preservative-free ophthalmic medications? [...] Sterile manufacturing is continuously monitored and governed by current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) standards that oversee every stage of production. 

Single-use ophthalmic vials are designed with a specific purpose: open, administer as prescribed and discard — even when liquid remains. Once opened, the sterile barrier becomes compromised. Replacing the cap does not recreate the original manufacturing conditions or restore the product’s integrity established during production.
